name: Tutoring business
blurb: Teach students one-to-one or in small groups, in person or online, paid per session
title: How to Start a Tutoring Business (In Person or Online)
description: How a tutoring or online tutoring business makes money, what you need, who it suits, safeguarding and platform risks, and how to test it with a few students.
h1: How to start a tutoring business
answer: A tutoring business teaches students one-to-one or in small groups, in person or online, and charges per session or per package. You mainly need subject knowledge, a way to teach and a few first students, so startup costs are low. The catches are uneven demand around exams and holidays, last-minute cancellations, and safeguarding rules when you work with children.

body: Most tutors charge per hour or per session, often with discounted packages paid in advance. Exam preparation, specialist subjects and adult learners such as professionals or language students can command more than general homework help. Small groups earn more per hour but need more preparation.
Margin goes to unpaid preparation time, travel for in-person lessons, platform commission if you teach through a marketplace, and sessions lost to cancellations.

ul: Strong knowledge of your subject and level, and the patience to explain it several ways.
For online tutoring: a reliable computer, camera, microphone, stable internet and a whiteboard or screen-sharing tool.
Teaching materials, practice papers and a simple way to track each student's progress.

Safeguarding checks: rules differ by country. Families and agencies may ask for a criminal record check, such as a DBS check in the UK, and you should have clear rules about meeting children, online contact and parents being present.
Local paperwork: registration as self-employed or as a business where you live, and terms covering payment and cancellations.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People who enjoy explaining and seeing progress
Teachers, graduates or specialists with a niche
People who want daytime-only hours (most students are free after school)
Anyone who needs steady income through every holiday

ul: Seasonality: demand often bunches before exams and drops in holidays.
Cancellations: without a written cancellation policy, missed sessions become unpaid time.
Platform dependence: marketplaces bring students but take commission and control your visibility.
Safeguarding: working with children carries responsibility; follow good practice and keep communication through parents where possible.
Client churn: students leave once their exam is over, so you need a steady flow of new ones.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Pick one subject and level you can teach well.
Tutor two or three students from your network at a real price for a month.
Search local listings and tutoring platforms to see what tutors in your subject offer.
Ask parents or students what made them choose a tutor and what they would pay.
Post one clear offer in local community groups or at a school noticeboard and count enquiries.
Register as self-employed or as a business and get any background check families will expect.
Write terms covering prices, packages, payment in advance and cancellations.
Prepare a first-session assessment so you can show progress later.
Choose in-person, online or both, and set up the tools for each.
Ask satisfied families for reviews and referrals, especially before exam seasons.

faq.q: Do I need a teaching qualification to tutor?
faq.a: In many countries private tutoring is not a regulated profession, so a qualification is not legally required. Parents often look for one, or for strong grades and experience, so be clear about your background.

faq.q: Is online tutoring better than in-person?
faq.a: Online tutoring removes travel and widens your reach, but competition is broader. In-person tutoring is easier to win locally through referrals. Many tutors do both.

faq.q: How do I find my first tutoring students?
faq.a: Start with your own network, local community groups, school noticeboards and tutoring platforms. Good results and word of mouth from parents usually bring the next students.
